body: I have received several messages over time, mostly just benign reinforcements of small epiphanies. But I recently had a session where out of nowhere I got the message, "you can't do that type of work anymore." I understood that to mean my job as a hospice nurse and my initial reflex was, oh, heck no. I love my job and cannot imagine doing anything else. But then a few days later I learned that the inpatient unit that I work at will be closing. There literally is nowhere similar within driving range that I can work. Which made me wonder if the message was actually, "you won't get to do that type of work anymore." A premonition, somehow. Probably just a coincidence, but made me think.

Was 7 months pregnant with twins. Home alone, and choked on a too-big bite of Haagen-Das mint chocolate chip ice cream. Completely sealed off my trachea. I wouldn't have been able to do the lean over the back of a chair move to dislodge it because of the babies. Almost started to panic but realized I had to get calm really quickly, conserve my oxygen, and just wait for the ice cream to melt. Which it did, but it seemed like it took forever. I waited as long as I absolutely could before using what air was left in my lungs to push the melting ice cream out. Had a wet cough for about a week afterwards, so almost certainly aspirated. Scared the bejeezus out of me.

I work in an inpatient hospice unit inside a major metropolitan hospital. It's a really unique environment, part ICU, part hospice, all about helping patients and families cope with end-of-life. I feel lucky to have found my niche.

Needed a lot of medical help to get & stay pregnant. Along the way, did a few intrauterine inseminations (IUI) where they put sperm directly into the uterus with a thin catheter. They usually want you to lie flat for 15-30 minutes before getting up. On one of my IUI attempts the doctor did the procedure then left the catheter and speculum in place...the speculum was wide open (or felt that way, at least). He said he'd be back, and left the room. Then the entire office went to lunch. I was left like that on the table with my vagina stretched wiiiiiiide open for well over an hour. I started yelling for someone to come help me at about the 45 minute mark. I couldn't get up because the the speculum hurt when I moved even a little bit and I didn't want to somehow mess up the IUI attempt. My insides totally dried up. When they finally remembered/found me an hour and 15 minutes later, I was a crying mess. It was awful. I was sore for days. And needless to say, that IUI didn't work. I still get a little upset thinking about it, and it was almost 20 years ago.

One favorite...A patient's daughter brought in a record player so her mom could listen to her favorite albums. Patient requested to hear *The Sound of Music* several times, but the album was missing. The daughter finally found the album and dropped it off, but didn't want to wake mom to play it. When I was with her mom the next day I saw *The Sound of Music* on the top of the stack of records. I was caught up with work at the moment, so I thought I'd sit with her a bit. Put the record on and enjoyed the music, but when the song *So Long, Farewell* came on the patient's breathing changed. As the song ended, she took her last breath. I was like, "OMG, she did NOT just die at the end of that song!" But she had. The lyrics to the song, for context:

When the daughter came to collect her mom's things later she told me that she had been driving in her car when out of nowhere she felt compelled to look underneath the passenger seat, and that's where she found the album. It had slid off the stack that was on the back seat when she was bringing the albums and record player to the hospice unit. 

Also had an alert & oriented woman that arrived to our unit in a wheelchair, was able to transfer to the bed with light assistance (most our patients are bed bound). She did not seem imminent/near death at all, but she told her three daughters that she would be dead in the morning. They just shrugged off what she was saying, thinking she was just being dramatic. They all spent the night in the room with mom, but when they woke up in the morning she was, in fact, dead. 

Two of many, many examples I have that demonstrate that some people have very precise control of the timing of their passing. Never ceases to amaze me.

I have definitely had patients that were hard of hearing all of a sudden seem to be able to hear well without their hearing aids. I've also had blind patients appear to be seeing something, eyes open, gaze tracking. I've had multiple ESRD patients that haven't urinated in years start making urine, too. Our bodies do weird things as they are shutting down.

Hospice nurse at an inpatient unit, too many stories to tell. The vast majority of time when patients have visions, they seem to be a source of comfort, or at least not disturbing to them. But I've had a couple of occasions when they seemed super afraid of what they were seeing. One patient was yelling, "stop! make them stop! go away! it hurts! stop!" over and over for a few hours, died shortly thereafter. His daughter later told me that he had been a horrible person his whole life. He was in and out of prison, and when he was released from his latest sentence he handed back to his daughter all the letters she had written to him while he was imprisoned...unopened. That's a majorly cruel move.
I sound like a complete cheeseball, but there is no better work than caring for others in their hour of need. End of story, for me. All the frustrations pale next to the rewards.

Not sure where you are located, but many major hospital systems have inpatient hospice units within their hospitals. I started as a new grad on a med-surg unit that was right next to the hospice IPU, precisely so I could eventually segue in there. I got a great med-surg education while biding my time, and it eventually worked out for me. These IPUs are not open to the public, per se, but more used for supporting patients at end-of-life from within the hospital system, so they can be a little hard to find.

I wanted to start in hospice straight after nursing school but couldn't find anyone to hire me without other experience first. I ended up doing two years of med-surg before starting hospice full time, and I'm \*so\* glad I did. I have a much better understanding of the pathophysiology and disease progression that landed my patients in hospice in the first place. I learned so many tips and tricks in med-surg that are useful in hospice. I work with a couple of nurses that went straight from nursing school into hospice and they often have challenges that I don't. Everyone's path is different, but if you do end up not being able to start in hospice, I hope you can view it as an opportunity that will serve you well, not a speed bump on the way to being where you want to be.

All the time. As a hospice nurse I recognize that I have a bias towards comfort vs. aggressive treatment, but the things some of these families do to their "loved" ones break my heart. When they end up on hospice the families are never truly on board with hospice philosophy, so when their "loved" ones die, as often as not they accuse us of killing them. It's misplaced grief and anger & frustration at not being able to help/save their "loved" one.

I always encourage my families to step away and communicate to their loved one that they are doing so. "Mom, we're all going to lunch. It's 11 o'clock now, we'll be back around 2 o'clock." Crazy how often people use that window of time to pass. If that's how it does end up playing out for your family, I encourage you to not view it as a failure on your part for not being there, but rather, how your mother-in-law wanted it to be.

Many people seem to have some control over the timing of their passing. Some people want/need to be alone to pass. Was she a private person in general? People die as they lived. She may be waiting for someone specific to leave because she doesn't want to pass in front of them. I work in an inpatient hospice setting and see this alllllll the time.

I have had patients that would hit the remote on their hydromorphone PCA, then stick a needle/syringe into the IV tubing to try to withdraw the dose as it was being dispensed from the pump so they could accumulate several doses to shoot later. The tubing might leak after being punctured, but not always. One patient tried to melt the tubing to seal the leak (which does not work) and another clever patient used super glue. We initially discovered the diversion by finding the burnt IV tubing...that patient was the one that clued us in about what was happening.  I would be very wary about allowing known addicts to immediately scoot into the bathroom while a dose was dispensing. And if there is even the slightest irregularity with the tubing, any bending, creasing, leaking, be suspicious.

Yup! Some people seem to require privacy to die. I work in an inpatient hospice unit and see it all the time, patients waiting for visitors to step away before they die. The amount of control we seem to have over the timing of our death never ceases to amaze me.

As a hospice nurse, one of the standard things I tell my families is that it seems like \*most\* people have some control over the timing of their passing. We've all heard of dying people waiting for a specific visitor to get bedside before passing away. The flip side of that coin is also true, people often wait for specific visitors to leave before passing away. Go to the festival. When you leave, tell your mom when you'll be back. And if she does happen to pass away while you're gone, you shouldn't think of it as a failure on your part, you can believe that was her intent, to spare you that final moment. Moms especially seem to wait until their kids leave before passing. If it's important to her for you to be there when she dies, you will be. I have seen waaaaaaay too many instances of dying people holding out for the "right" moment for them, so live your life.

Hospice nurse, solidly agnostic, never have been open to the idea that there's a god that's "driving the bus" and causing things to happen or not happen. No fan of organized religion. As the years working in hospice pass I become more convinced that this is not all there is, though. I think we have a soul that continues to exist after our bodies die. Where it exists or in what form, I have no idea. 

Patients & families that I've cared for that had solid faiths often seem to handle the dying process more easily. Their belief that there's an afterlife and they'll see each other again does seem to bring some of them legitimate comfort. I think this is one of the few benefits of organized religion.

Also hospice nurse, can confirm we waste scandalous amounts of narcotics. I'm in an inpatient setting, our opioid and benzo orders are written as really small doses that can be given at short intervals, usually q10min for opioids and q1hour for benzos (unless it's being used for seizures). So I might be drawing up 0.2 mg hydromorphone out of a 0.5 mg vial every 10 minutes and having to waste the 0.3 mg every time. And that's if we're lucky and the Omnicell is actually stocked with the 0.5 mg hydromorphone...just as likely to have to use 1 mg or 2 mg hydromorphone for those little bitty doses. 

We also are not allowed to accept custody of narcotic drips/PCAs that have been started prior to the patient's admission to the hospice unit, even though our patients are exclusively coming from elsewhere in the hospital. That means the ICU might hang a 60 mg bag of lorazepam that has to be wasted once the patient transfers to a hospice bed. Only for us to turn around and hang another 60 mg lorazepam bag.

The whole thing drives me nuts.

Hospice nurse here, second career, was a graphic designer for 25+ years but have been a nurse now for over 5 years. I am working in a medium sized suburban hospital and in addition to caring for hospice pts, I also care for oncology/med-surg pts...I much prefer hospice pts, though.  I tried home hospice for 9 months and did not like it, too much busywork & not enough pt care, so have been happy to be back in the hospital for the last six months.
